title: What an Agent Can Prove It Did
description: Nine tools that replace trust with evidence: audit trails, signed receipts, deterministic gates and checks that compare a claim with what actually changed.

images.alt: A team reviewing logs and audit records on a shared screen
images.caption: Signed records and deterministic gates turn agent activity into something you can check later.

content:
# What an Agent Can Prove It Did

An agent that reports success is telling you a story. The nine tools in this group start from the position that the story is not enough. They record tool calls, compare claimed changes with real ones, seal results into records that can be checked offline, and in several cases stop a call before it runs. The shared idea is not detection. It is evidence: something deterministic, local and inspectable that exists after the model has finished talking, and that does not depend on asking another model whether the first one behaved.

## Reading the record afterwards

[[link:/tools/2301|Stroq]] is a local security platform for coding agents that begins with an audit of sessions you already had. It reads the last 30 days of Claude Code and Codex sessions, your key files and the folders the agent worked in, then prints key names and never values. It writes nothing but a small cache and sends nothing. From there it can install hooks that judge every tool call before it runs, denying curl piped into a shell and outbound calls carrying a known secret, and asking you first when a command repeats text the agent read. A console on the local machine shows each decision with the text that triggered it, the rule and the outcome. It is Apache-2.0, needs Node 22 or newer, and can replay old sessions against policy without installing anything.

[[link:/tools/2302|Shield KYA]] takes a similar shape but is explicit about where enforcement lives. It records every tool call on a local dashboard and by default denies a short list of destructive commands, secret reads and exfiltration; everything else is recorded, not blocked. Local hooks fail open. Real blocking and human approval run on the MCP policy path against a hosted workspace, where an agent that asks first gets Allow, Review or Deny and Review waits for a person. One useful engineering detail is that eval-tool, wrap and invoke exit non-zero on DENY, so a chained command cannot quietly skip the gate. It is MIT, starts with one command and needs Node 22 or newer.

[[link:/tools/2309|Apgar]] applies the same discipline to releases rather than individual calls. It watches the first hours of every agent release and tells you whether behaviour got worse than the release before it: more tool errors, retries and loops, fewer tool calls, shorter answers, higher cost or latency. It works from OpenTelemetry or Langfuse traces you already collect, across all traffic, with no LLM judge, no dataset and no stored prompt or completion text. Tag each deploy with a release attribute and you get one Slack message or webhook. It is Apache-2.0 and self-hosted on Docker Compose or Kubernetes.

## Comparing the claim with the change

The sharpest example here is [[link:/tools/2303|Deedglass]], whose opening line is a small horror story: an agent said it updated one row, and Postgres changed 301. It sits between agents and the systems they change. Rules decide each tool call, a check compares what the system really changed with what the agent reported, and each result is labeled as claimed, checked or proven and as matching, not matching or impossible to check. Every result is sealed as a signed record anyone can verify offline, and the tool can undo the rows an action changed. It runs on your own computer with no account and no Docker, and a replay scene demonstrates the mismatch in under 30 seconds. The Apache-2.0 core includes every feature free.

[[link:/tools/2304|Nomos]] targets a different kind of dishonesty, the agent that makes a failing test pass by weakening it. It is a transactional Go runtime between any coding agent and a Git repository, isolating tasks in disposable git worktree sandboxes and separating INT specs from SUB code so the agent cannot rewrite a spec to excuse broken code. It uses 42 polyglot AST quality gates to block deleted assertions and hollow shims before merge, pins its configuration to trunk, keeps receipt-gated SQLite memory, and releases through atomic two-phase commit. It works with Claude Code, Cursor, Antigravity, OpenCode, Windsurf and Aider, and its enforcement lives in compiled Go, Git hooks and AST exit codes outside the model context window. It is a heavy layer with its own vocabulary, but the failure mode it names is real.

[[link:/tools/2305|Maat]] moves the boundary down to the kernel. It is an open-source MCP server and toolkit for diagnosing Ubuntu systems, reading state from inside a strictly confined snap with read-oriented permissions and no network access at all. Fixes become typed, reviewable plans approved through polkit, the same mechanism that guards systemctl restart. It shows the evidence a plan relies on and flags citations the model invented, then records every step in a tamper-evident trail. It ships with maat-bench, an open benchmark of deliberately broken Ubuntu machines for measuring both root-cause finding and behaviour when logs try to hijack the model. It is a developer preview, and the first results come from two small local models on easy scenarios, which the project says to read as a first data point rather than a ranking.

## Deterministic gates instead of judges

[[link:/tools/2306|Bouncer]] is a local MCP proxy that denies an agent's send and share calls when the destination first appeared in untrusted tool output. If a poisoned email, ticket or document supplied an address and the agent later tries to email or share to it, the call is denied. The match is literal and no LLM decides anything; destinations it cannot trace go to a human, and allowlisted or approved ones pass. It also confines paths, checks arguments against regex rules, applies per-session call budgets and refuses tools that were not present at startup. Every allow, deny and ask becomes a JSON line in an audit log that can be turned into a review pack. The honesty of the README is worth quoting: in an AgentDojo run Bouncer allowed no send at all, so legitimate sending tasks went from four of six to zero of six. It is version 0.1.4, early, and covers MCP over stdio on one machine.

[[link:/tools/2307|Weir]] hunts a narrower leak. You plant a unique fake key wherever a real one would live, run your agent's own flows against a local fake model, then search spans, logs, console output and model traffic for that exact value. It never prints the key. In Claude Code a status-line segment counts how many real credentials entered the session or left in a tool call, and an optional hook replaces known keys in Read, Bash, Grep, Glob or WebFetch results before the model sees them. It found a credential-leak issue in MLflow, runs in a pull request through a GitHub Action, and installs with pip. The README also notes the awkward edge case that very large tool outputs can still be saved whole to the session folder by Claude Code.

[[link:/tools/2308|Spring AI Privacy Guardrails]] brings the same thinking to Java applications. It tokenizes detected PII before it reaches the model, reveals only the originals a given tool needs, and protects the tool result again before the model answers. Tool authorization limits visibility and execution using the current user's permissions through Spring Security, while content inspection can use rules, a local ONNX classifier or an HTTP guard model. The three features work independently, decisions and tool execution can be recorded in Langfuse, and PII detection uses Presidio and JVM-local OpenNLP. It needs Java 17 or later, Spring AI 2.0 and Spring Boot 4.0.

## Why evidence is the common thread

What unites these nine is a refusal to make another model the referee. Traces, hashes, signed records, AST exit codes, kernel permissions and literal string matches all share a property: you can check them yourself, later, without trusting the thing being checked. That matters more as sessions get longer and agents get more authority. It also imposes a cost. Several of these tools slow work down, block legitimate calls, or need a hosted plane for real enforcement, and the ones that are most strict say so in their own documentation. A gate that denies everything is safe but useless. The useful middle ground seems to be the one these projects are converging on: record everything, block a short explicit list, and send ambiguous cases to a person.
tldr: Stroq, Shield KYA, Deedglass, Nomos, Maat, Bouncer, Weir, Spring AI Privacy Guardrails and Apgar all produce verifiable evidence about agent behaviour.
